data.text:
Can Copper be the next Gold or Silver? 

We can’t comment on that, but there is an incredible story from the 1990s that every trader should know.👇

Yasuo Hamanaka, nicknamed “Mr. Copper,” was a trader at Japan’s Sumitomo Corporation who almost controlled the global copper market. 

It all began in 1985 when his boss, Saburo Shimizu, lost $60 million on a failed copper deal in the Philippines.

Shimizu quit, but Hamanaka was promoted in 1986 to head copper trading. Instead of stopping, he hid losses in secret ledgers, forged documents, and shredded evidence. 

Hamanaka wasn’t just any trader, under him Sumitomo controlled about 5 percent of the global copper market giving him another nickname Mr. Five Percent

To manipulate prices without exposure, he relied on forward contracts on the London Metal Exchange (LME), which had looser rules than U.S. exchanges like COMEX. 

He borrowed over $1.5 billion from banks including Merrill Lynch, J.P. Morgan, and Chase Manhattan and accumulated both futures and physical copper warrants, which are basically ownership slips for stored copper.

By the early 1990s, Hamanaka teamed with U.S. traders like David Campbell, who ran RST Resources. 

They bought copper warrants from mines in Zambia and traded them back and forth to make it appear legitimate. 

Paul Scully, a compliance officer at DLT Inc. spotted the fakes in 1991 and warned his boss, David Threlkeld. Scully died mysteriously later that year, ruled an accident, adding a strange layer to the affair.

By 1995, Hamanaka controlled 93% of the LME’s copper warrants, almost half of the world’s deliverable supply. 

Prices surged from $2,500 to $2,800 per ton, squeezing traders who bet against copper. The electronics boom, construction demand, and mine disruptions amplified the spike. 

Banks extended massive credit lines and even created special instruments, like Merrill Lynch’s Commodity Inventory Purchase Obligations, to support his positions. 

The collapse began in 1996 when odd warehouse movements triggered regulatory attention. 

Sumitomo discovered Hamanaka’s secret account on May 9, fired him, and by June 5 he confessed everything. 

On June 13, the world learned of $1.8 billion in hidden losses, totaling $2.6 billion. Copper prices plunged from $2,800 to $1,800 per ton in a matter of weeks. 

Hamanaka disappeared for a time, resurfaced, and eventually served eight years in prison. 

Sumitomo recovered $500 million from banks and paid $150 million in fines. Campbell and partners faced investigations too.

This dramatic saga is now famously known as the Sumitomo Copper Affair.

Even decades later, traders study Hamanaka’s audacious positions to understand the impact of leverage, market control, and how a single individual can move global prices.
